extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy students, and performers learning the Greg Dean method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for writing, structuring, and performing stand-up comedy using Greg Dean's methods (joke structure, timing, material selection, and stagecraft). Intended to help comedians create, order, rehearse, and present material effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 LPMs (Laughs Per Minute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Laughs Per Minute. 5 or more laughs per minute is the professional standard for stand-up comedy shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great stand up comedy routine should get at least 5 LPMs. Use LPMs to evaluate pacing and density of laughs in routines and shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABCs material rating system
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating system that gives values to jokes within routines, or routines within shows with A being the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A material = funniest jokes/routines; B material = second-best; C material = weakest. Example: 'I'll start my show with my B material, do some crowd work, then end with my A material.' Use this to select and order material.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCAs (order of material)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective order for placing jokes within routines or routines within a shows: B material first, C material in the middle, and A material to close the routine or show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BCAs to keep audience engaged and end with your strongest material. Example: 'My show is funnier at the beginning than it is at the end, so I'm going to order it differently using the BCAs system so I'll end with my best jokes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-5 and 10-minute routine readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Three most common lengths of routines or shows, in minutes, which comedians need to have prepared and ready to perform upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare usable 3-5 minute and 10-minute routines for booking requests and open mic opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Structure (Greg Dean's 5 mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Greg Dean model of joke structure, there are 5 mechanisms which connect the Setup and Punchline: 1st Story, Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation, and 2nd Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the five mechanisms to analyze, fix, and write jokes. The structure explains how Setup and Punchline are linked and why misdirection works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connector (1 thing with 2 interpretations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke structure mechanism at the center of all comedy, defined as 1 thing with at least 2 interpretations; usually an ambiguity used to write a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a Connector (ambiguity) in the setup and craft the punchline as a Reinterpretation. Fully explained in Greg Dean's works; use Connector as the primary device for misdirection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target Assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the five joke structure mechanisms: the expected interpretation of the Connector, established by the Setup to create misdirection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the Target Assumption clearly so the audience accepts it; then the punchline must shatter that assumption to create surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation (Punchline's mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unexpected interpretation of the Connector, expressed in the Punchline to create surprise and laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the punchline as a Reinterpretation compatible with the Connector but surprising compared to the Target Assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1st Story (setup scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in audience's minds based upon receiving a joke's Setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft setups that create vivid, believable 1st Stories so the Target Assumption is clear; 1st Story anchors the audience's expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2nd Story (punchline scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in the audience's minds based upon receiving a joke's Punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2nd Story created by the punchline must be unexpected yet compatible with the Connector so the joke lands and makes sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup (establish Target Assumption/misdirection)
rubrics_metrics.description: First of two parts of one-liner jokes designed to misdirect the audience; part that establishes the Target Assumption or expected meaning of the Connector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite the setup so it more clearly misdirects the audience and establishes the intended Target Assumption. Avoid telegraphing (giving away the punchline) by over-explaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline (creates surprise/laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section Two / Punchline communicates a Reinterpretation, the unexpected interpretation of the Connector, which makes the Setup’s expected interpretation wrong, shattering the Target Assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punchlines should deliver the Reinterpretation cleanly; consider tags afterwards to extend the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag (immediate short punchline after punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional short punchline immediately following a punchline that does not require a new setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tags to pile on laughs after a strong punchline without needing a new setup. Tags can increase LPM and strengthen the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling joke structure (scene, POVs, acting, staging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes in storytelling have the same setup/punchline structure as one-liners but require scene work, space work, object work, situations, relationships, tenses, psychology, acting, and staging using the POVs of Narrator, Self, and Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing storytelling jokes, distribute setup, punchline, and tags among POVs; develop acting and staging skills. Storytelling requires more performance skills than one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomy of Funny Storytelling / POVs (Narrator, Self, Character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greg Dean’s model of the three performance roles/points of view used in stand-up storytelling: Narrator POV, Self POV, and Character POV. Comedians will often become all 3 POVs when storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to shift between POVs to create scenes and act them out; Narrator POV sets the scene, Self/Character POVs are used for act-outs and scene work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act out / Scene work
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene work in a stand-up routine where the comedian portrays all the roles (Narrator, Self, Character) and enacts a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use act outs to bring scenes to life; practice acting choices, physicality, and vocal changes. Act outs allow storytelling joke structure to function fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / Comic timing / Comedy timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempo, rhythm, and emphasis of material and response in a feedback loop between comedians and their audiences during a performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop tempo and rhythm with the audience; timing affects when to pause, deliver tags, and move on. Good timing can make or break jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a beat / Pause
rubrics_metrics.description: Pause or break during a comedy show for purposes of delivery and comic timing, often between the Setup and Punchline or after a Punchline to let the audience laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pauses to allow the audience to process setups and to laugh after punchlines. Proper pauses prevent stepping on laughs and improve LPMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay in the bit / Don't step on laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: After a Punchline, stop talking and remain in the same emotion/state to give the audience permission and space to laugh and to maintain momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staying in the bit prevents 'step on laughs' or 'talk over laughs' which kill the laugh. Let the audience laugh before continuing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk over laughs / Step on laughs (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: After delivery of a Punchline, when the comedian continues to speak instead of taking a pause, interrupting the audience's laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid talking over laughs; it reduces the size and duration of laughter and harms momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurry a joke (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating a joke faster than the audience can comprehend the Setup's relationship to the Punchline, which can diminish or kill the laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rush delivery; trust the setup and give the audience time to build the Target Assumption and process the Reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraphing (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causing the audience to guess the Punchline before it's delivered, usually because the Setup has too much information or an acting choice that leads the audience prematurely to the idea of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid telegraphing by tightening setups and ensuring misdirection. The setup should misdirect, not reveal the punchline early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery (intonation, inflection, pace, timing, character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of intonation, inflection, pace, timing, and character idiosyncrasies in presenting comedy material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong delivery enhances jokes; practice voice, pacing, and character choices to support the joke rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal process / avoid improper rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper rehearsal (e.g. rote repetition) can code jokes into internal self-talk (Broca area) causing performers to rely on internal speech to recall jokes; 'talking head' delivery is a risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearse with emotion, physicality, and in varied contexts to avoid mechanical delivery and improve recall and adaptability on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Map / Joke Mine / Joke Prospector Writing System
rubrics_metrics.description: Greg Dean's step-by-step joke writing system: Joke Map (topic → punch-premise → setup-premise → setups) and Joke Mine (use setups and the 5 mechanisms to write punchlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the system to create many setups and then mine them using Connector, Target Assumption, and Reinterpretation. Use it as a repeatable writing workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke premise / Setup-Premise / Punch-Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises are the message or negative opinion from which to write jokes; Setup-Premise is constructed opposite the Punch-Premise to generate misdirection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clear premises to focus joke writing. Use premise steps in the Joke Map to generate reliable setups and punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hammock (placement strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique of placing weak or new stand-up material between two strong jokes or routines to support the newer material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hammocks to test new material without risking audience momentum; e.g., open with B, hammock new bit, close with A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph (evaluate & place jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual device with dots on paper for evaluating the effectiveness of jokes to determine their proper placement within routines or shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge jokes on a graph to identify strongest material and inform BCAs ordering and hammock placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke file / gag file
rubrics_metrics.description: An organized collection of jokes and routines (index cards or digital) used to store material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a joke/gag file to organize tested material, track versions, and select A/B/C ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting or altering material to fit a unique performing situation and different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust references, tone, and examples to match audience demographics and venue (e.g., cops, college students, corporate). Tailoring increases relevance and laugh rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean vs blue / x-rated material (audience suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean material: jokes with no curse words or inappropriate subjects suitable for network TV. Blue/X-rated: graphic sexual, scatological, and swear words not appropriate for network television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material appropriate to venue and booking (network TV vs late-night clubs). Beware of offending audiences; know when blue material is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurt line / edgy material (risk boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurt line: subjective tipping point when the pain within comedy becomes real and turns mood into drama. Edgy: material dealing with hurtful subjects while maintaining a comedic tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edgy material can work if it stays on the funny side of the hurt line; crossing it turns comedy into drama. Use caution and test material in safer rooms first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd work (audience interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When comedians ask questions of the audience then banter with the intent to find laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crowd work to find spontaneous laughs and to warm/engage an audience, but prepare comeback/heckler lines and be adaptable to audience responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heckler lines / preparing to shut down hecklers
rubrics_metrics.description: Insult jokes comedians write, collect, and memorize to use on different kinds of hecklers to get them to shut up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a repertoire of heckler lines (smart comebacks) tailored for types of interruptions; use them to regain control of the room while creating laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housekeeping / MC duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties of the MC: make announcements, promote future shows, recognize birthdays, point out exits/restrooms, calm hecklers, sell merchandise, run raffles, give curtain calls, and end shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an MC, perform housekeeping clearly and professionally to keep the show running and maintain audience safety and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth on / smooth off (stage entrance/exits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practices for getting on stage and off stage to ensure well-run shows (phrase coined by Jerry Seinfeld).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan entrances and exits to avoid awkwardness; practice a clean 'get on' and 'get off' to maintain show momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the light / respect time cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Signal (get the light) that indicates the comedian has one minute left or it's time to end the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect lighting/time cues from stage management; wrap up promptly when signaled to maintain professionalism and bookings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set list / show list
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullet point reminders of the order of the jokes or routines to be done in a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a printed or phone set list to keep order; helps with pacing, callbacks, and remembering tags and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage time (experience & duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: What comedians need in front of audiences to get experience and learn their craft; also refers to the duration in minutes comedians get to perform at each show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek frequent stage time to test material and improve timing; track minutes per show to build 3-5/10 minute routines and increase chops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hack / comic's clichés (originality requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hack: comics who perform overused and cliché topics and jokes with overacted delivery without relating to the audience. Comic's clichés: overused phrases and physical idiosyncrasies betraying lack of originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hacky material and clichéd delivery; strive for fresh premises and authentic voice. Hackiness is a major negative signal to audiences and peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clapter (applause vs laugh) — negative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke designed to get an audience to applaud and agree rather than laugh; term usually used negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of clapter: applause-for-agreement often signals content that appeals rhetorically but won't produce genuine laughs. Aim for laughter rather than applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare multiple venue-targeted materials (4 Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: 4 Cs = Clubs, Colleges, Cruise ships, and Corporations — four venues where stand-up comedians can get work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and tailor material suited to each of the 4 Cs (e.g., clean corporate bits, topical college material) to expand booking opportunities.
